A '''Heyting field''' is one of the inequivalent ways in [[constructive mathematics]] to capture the [[classical logic|classical]] notion of a [[field (mathematics)|field]]. It is essentially a field with an [[apartness relation]]. 

==Definition==
A [[commutative ring]] is a Heyting field if it is a field in the sense that
* <math>\neg(0=1)</math>
* Each non-invertible element is zero
and if it is moreover [[local ring|local]]: Not only does the non-invertible <math>0</math> not equal the invertible <math>1</math>, but the following disjunctions are granted more generally
* Either <math>a</math> or <math>1-a</math> is [[unit (ring theory)|invertible]] for every <math>a</math>

The third axiom may also be formulated as the statement that the algebraic "<math>+</math>" transfers invertibility to one of its inputs: If <math>a+b</math> is invertible, then either <math>a</math> or <math>b</math> is as well. 

===Relation to classical logic===
The structure defined without the third axiom may be called a weak Heyting field. Every such structure with decidable equality being a Heyting field is equivalent to excluded middle. Indeed, classically all fields are already local.

==Discussion==
An apartness relation is defined by writing <math>a \# b</math> if <math>a-b</math> is invertible. This relation is often now written as <math>a\neq b</math> with the warning that it is not equivalent to <math>\neg(a=b)</math>.

The assumption <math>\neg(a=0)</math> is then generally not sufficient to construct the inverse of <math>a</math>. However, <math>a \# 0</math> is sufficient.

==Example==
The prototypical Heyting field is the [[real number]]s.
